text: Exp 1: The experiment is divided into two parts. In each part, CSA is evaluated with a different set of problem samples. The objective is to explore how CSA performance varies when the problem size (number of features per model) and type of constraints vary. In the first part, the 18 algorithm configurations are executed with samples of models of different sizes, ranging from 10 features to 450 features, increasing the number in steps of 10 (i.e., 45 total samples). Each experiment step is performed with a sample of 200 problem instances, and the average value is computed in order to reduce the fluctuations due to randomness (e.g., the random seeds used to generate problem instances). In the second part, the 18 CSA configurations are executed with 5 samples of 200 problems each one. The number of features per model is fixed to 30 to focus on the influence of model constraints on the performance. This number was selected from the average number of features per model reported in Table 6. From one sample to another we vary the type of constraints incorporated to the models. The configurations of these constraints per sample are described below. _Exp 2: The experiment comprises the execution of the 8 algorithms previously mentioned (GAFES, Greedy, and the 6 CSA approximate configurations) with a set of samples of problem instances. Each sample consists of a set of 882 problem instances generated by using the models of the SPLOT repository. Since GAFES and Greedy algorithms only support basic CTCs (i.e., constraints with 2 features at most), in this experiment non-basic CTCs, which are the 17.26% of CTCs, are removed from models. Problem instances include a linear objective to be maximized and a single linear inequality restriction as global constraint, since this is the problem formalization supported by both algorithms. To this end, models are extended with 2 randomly generated attributes per features (a f , b f ), using a uniform distribution over (0, 1). One attribute is used to define the linear objective function, and the other one to define the inequality restriction. The experiment is carried out with 4 different samples of problems, each one with a different value of restriction ratio. In the first sample, the restriction ratio is equal to 1 (100%), so that the restriction cannot be violated by any solution. The other three samples use restriction ratios of 90%, 80% and 70%, respectively. By reducing the value of the restriction ratio, the problem becomes more restrictive and harder to solve, since less combinations of features can satisfy the constraint. Thus, by using different ratios, we can observe how the performance of approximate algorithms degrades as the problem becomes harder. _Exp 3: The experiment comprises the execution of the 8 algorithms previously mentioned (0-1 LP, BoolOpt and 6 CSA exact configurations) with a set of samples of problem instances. Similar to the previous experiment, a sample consists of a set of 882 problem instances generated by using the models of the SPLOT repository. Since 0-1 LP supports linear functions, problems are stated as the optimization of a linear objective function (|O F | = 1) with a variable number of linear inequality restrictions (|GC| = n). The first sample contains instances with 0 inequality restrictions, and the other samples contain instances with 1, 2 and 5 inequality restrictions, with a fixed restriction ratio of 90%. _Exp 4: We run the experiment with 2 samples of problem instances, each one with a different distribution of feature interactions. Similar to previous experiments, each sample consists of a set of 882 problem instances generated by using the models of the SPLOT repository enriched with attributes generated by Thor. In sample #1, models contain 1 interaction per feature, all of degree 2. In sample #2, models contain 2 interactions per feature: 67% of degree 2, 23% of degree 3 and 10% of degree 4. No inequality restrictions are considered, and the objective function is a multi-linear polynomial function including one term for each feature and interaction attribute generated by Thor.

text: The family-based mutant-detection methodology introduced in Sect. 3.3 allows for measuring the effectiveness of different kinds of PL analysis strategies in general, and sample-based PL testing in particular. To this end, we first derive a set of mutants from a PL implementation (cf. Sect. 3.2) using code- mutation operators and mapping-mutation operators . To measure effectiveness for a given sample, we investigate how many of the generated mutants are detectable by at least one test configuration in the sample. As outlined in Algorithm 1, we generate an (abstract) test suite for each mutant contain- ing a set of test cases detecting the mutant. text: To answer the posed questions, for each FM, we executed the following steps: (1) Mutants generation: to generate the mutants, the operators were applied with the application percentage of 100%. text: Our model difference algorithm was evaluated using the methodology from [5]. For a given pair of product feature models, M1 and M2, we define Me as the set of anticipated changes and Mr as the set of changes identified by our approach. Both Me and Mr are structured as {<f1, f2, changetype>}, where f1 is a feature from M1, f2 is its corresponding feature in M2, and 'changetype' specifies whether the feature remained the same, was added, or was renamed. Following the differentiation process, a model merge algorithm was employed for integration. The accuracy of this merge was then assessed. A successful composition is characterized by minimizing both false positive (incorrect) and false negative (missed correct) merges. This balance was measured using precision and recall. Precision quantifies the correctness of the found compositions (correct compositions / total found compositions), while recall measures how thoroughly correct compositions were identified (correct compositions found / total correct compositions). The experiment utilized corpus 5 from UNIONmode, with the final results being the average derived from seven distinct data sets.

text: To evaluate participants' understanding of programs, we devised a set of tasks comprising two static tasks (S1, S2) and four maintenance tasks (M1–M4). The static tasks required subjects to identify feature code. Specifically, in S1, they had to pinpoint all files containing code for a given feature and record their findings on a "grid template," which visually mapped code to features. For the color-coded version, feature names on the grid matched the source code's background color, while the ifdef version used a grid without background colors. S2 instructed participants to locate shared code, meaning code used by multiple features (e.g., SMSFeature & CopyPhoto). Locating feature code is a routine activity for developers learning an SPL or debugging, as bugs frequently trace back to particular features or their combinations, especially complex interactions in SPLs (Kästner 2010). For the maintenance tasks, we intentionally embedded various bugs within annotated code fragments. Through a pre-test with 7 students, we identified four bugs that were neither too easy nor too difficult, and then arranged them by increasing complexity. Each bug was presented with a description akin to what a user would submit in a bug-tracking system, also specifying the affected feature. This setup ensured we could assess the impact of background colors, as subjects would concentrate on the feature code and its associated colors, rather than unexplored code sections. For each task, participants needed to find the bug (identifying the class and method), explain its occurrence, and propose a fix. This information allowed us to determine if the bug's root cause was correctly identified. As an illustration, the first maintenance task (M1) involved a bug where pictures sorted by views in an album were still displayed unsorted, a problem found in the 'CountViews' feature within the PhotoListController class due to an empty bubbleSort method. Additionally, a warm-up task was included for subjects to become accustomed to the experimental setup (counting MobileMedia features), but its results were not considered for analysis. ... We utilized the same tasks from our initial experiment, including the warm-up task (W0), but altered the task sequence to M1, M3, S1, M4, M2, S2. This alternating pattern of static and maintenance tasks aimed to determine if participants would shift between different code representations as per our hypothesis. ... For measuring program comprehension, we developed several tasks, primarily static tasks, because our initial experiment showed that background colors helped with static tasks, but not maintenance tasks. However, we included a few maintenance tasks to confirm these earlier findings. In total, we had 10 tasks: two warm-up tasks (W1, W2) that were excluded from analysis, six static tasks (S1–S6), and two maintenance tasks (M1, M2). The static tasks were categorized into three types, with two tasks for each type: 1. Identifying all files where a specific feature was implemented (S1, S4). 2. Locating nested ifdef directives, which are important for understanding feature interactions (S2, S5). 3. Identifying all features present in a particular file (S3, S6). An example for a static task is S1: "Which files contain the feature CONFIG_XENO_OPT_STATS?" For maintenance tasks, we followed the same methodology as the first experiment, introducing bugs into the source code and providing participants with typical bug descriptions that included the feature selections where the bug occurred. We consulted an expert in C and Xenomai to ensure the bugs were characteristic of C programs. For instance, the first maintenance task (M1) was: "Unloading the PEAK parallel port dongle driver (XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG) leads to a segmentation fault. This issue arises when features CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN, CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000, and CONFIG_XENO_DRIVERS_CAN_SJA1000_PEAK_DNG are all selected. The bug was caused by an omitted null check in the code, specifically changing `if (ckfn && (err = ckfn(block)) != 0)` to `if ((err = ckfn(block)) != 0)`. If the `ckfn` variable is accessed when null, a segmentation fault occurs."

text: Following the methodology in [42], empirical tuning was conducted for NSGA-II and PAES using AGM-1 and AGM-3 to determine optimal population size, mutation rate, and crossover rate. The Hypervolume (HV) metric was employed for comparing tuning outcomes. Initial population size tests indicated that a population of 100 individuals performed as well as or better than populations of 50 or 70 for both algorithms. Consequently, NSGA-II versions and PAES's external archive were set to 100 individuals. Subsequently, mutation rates of {0.8, 0.9, 1.0} were evaluated, with 0.9 proving superior for both MOEAs. text: 3.2.1 First hypotheses: effect of stability on inconsistency rate In the first hypothesis, we speculate that a high variation of the design characteristics of the design models may lead to a higher incidence of inconsistencies; since, it increases the chance for an incorrect manipulation of the design charac- teristic by the composition heuristics. In fact, modifications fromsevereevolutionsmayleadthecompositionheuristicsto be ineffective or even prohibitive. In addition, these inconsis- tencies may also propagate. As a higher incidence of changes is found in unstable models, we hypothesize that unstable models tend to have a higher (or equal to) inconsistency rate than stable models. The first hypothesis evaluates whether the inconsistency rate in unstable models is significantly higher (or equal to) than in stable models. Thus, our hypotheses are summarized as follows: Null Hypothesis 1, H1−0: Stable design models have similar or higher inconsis- tency rate than unstable design models. H1−0:Rate(stabledesignmodels)≥Rate(unstabledesign models). Alternative Hypothesis 1, H1−1: Stabledesignmodels havealower inconsistencyratethan unstable design models. H1−1:Rate(stabledesignmodels)<Rate(unstabledesign models). By testing this first hypothesis, we evaluate if stability is a good indicator to identify the most critical MCM in term of inconsistency rate from a sequence of MCM produced from multiple software development teams. Hence, developers can then review the design models having a higher density of composition inconsistencies. We believe that this strategy is a more effective one than going through all MCM produced or assuming an overoptimistic position where all MCM pro- duced is a MAB. ... 3.2.2 Second hypothesis: effect of stability on developer effort As previously mentioned, developers tend to invest different quantity of effort to derive MAB from MCM. Today, model managers are unable to grasp how much effort this trans- formation can demand. This variation is because developers need to resolve different types of problems in a composed model, from a simple renaming of elements to complex mod- ifications in the structure of the composed model. In fact, the structure of the composed models may be affected in different ways during the composition, e.g., creating unex- pected interdependences between the model elements. Even worse, these modifications in the structure of the model may cause ripple effects, i.e., inconsistency propagation between the model elements. The introduction of one inconsistency can often lead to multiple other inconsistencies because of a “knock-on” effect. An example would be the inconsistency whereby a client component is missing an important opera- tion in the interface of a server component (see example in Sect. 2.4). This semantic inconsistency leads to a “knock- on” syntactic inconsistency if another component requires the operation. In the worst case, there may be long chains of inconsistencies all derived from a single inconsistency. Given a composed model at hand, developers need to know if they will invest little or too much effort to transform MCM into MAB, given the problem at hand. Based on this knowl- edge, they will be able to prioritize the review of the output composed models and to better comprehend the effort to be invested, e.g., reviewing the models that require higher effort first and those requiring less effort after. With this in mind, we are interested in understanding the possible difference of effort to resolve inconsistencies in stable and unstable design models. The expectation is that stable models require a lower developers’ effort to produce the output intended model. This expectation is based on the speculation that unstable mod- els may demand more restructuring modifications than stable models; hence, requiring more effort. This leads to the second null and alternative hypotheses as follows: Null Hypothesis 2, H2−0: Stable models require similar or higher effort to resolve inconsistencies than unstable models. H2−0: Effort(stable models) ≥Effort(unstable models). Alternative Hypothesis 2, H2−1: Stable models tend to require a lower inconsistency res- olution effort than unstable ones. H2−1: Effort(stable models) < Effort(unstable models). By testing this first hypothesis, we evaluate if stability is a useful indicator to identify the most critical effort-consuming cases in which severe semantic inconsistencies in archi- tectural components are more often. This knowledge helps model managers to allocate qualified developers to overcome the composition inconsistencies in MCM.

text: We use quantitative data to confirm our hypotheses, which are directly formulated from our research questions. To assess hypothesis validity, we conduct the following data analyses: RQ1 aims to quantify the variants that remain unchanged, are modified, or are newly introduced when advancing to the next SPL version, as determined by higher-order delta application reasoning. RQ2 explores the quantity of retest goals generated by our change impact analysis, which utilizes incremental model slicing. These retest goals signify that changes implemented in the model affect behavior that was previously tested across sequential variants and their versions. RQ3 involves a comparison between the number of test cases selected and produced by our framework and the number of test cases executed by the 'retest-all' approach (Yoo and Harman, 2007), with the goal of identifying any reduction in necessary test cases. Moreover, we evaluate the time consumed by both change impact analysis methods to gauge the efficiency of our selection technique, based on the cost model by Leung and White (1991). RQ4 evaluates the fault detection capability of our framework against that of 'retest-all' (Yoo and Harman, 2007). Since the two SPLs under study lack authentic fault histories, we create simulated faults by incorporating the changes made to a test model when transitioning to a subsequent variant or variant version. Fault derivation involves combining changes from model regression deltas (e.g., added transitions, source/target states of removed transitions) with randomly chosen transitions from the test model. These faults represent erroneous interactions between artifacts caused by modifications and their effect on common behavior. For each variant and its version, a corresponding set of these simulated faults is generated. Depending on the size of the fault set, we create a maximum number of distinct data sets, with each iteration involving a random selection of 10% of the faults to produce varied random fault data sets. The test cases designated for retesting by our framework, along with those for 'retest-all' (Yoo and Harman, 2007), are then executed to ascertain the fault detection rate. RQ5, mirroring RQ1, investigates the number of retest goals produced by our change impact analysis as an indicator of retest potential, but with the application of various testing orders to our approach. The testing orders for the initial SPL versions are calculated using established product prioritization techniques (Al-Hajjaji et al., 2017; Lity et al., 2017; Al-Hajjaji et al., 2014; Henard et al., 2014) as well as through random generation. For the random generation method, 100 product orders are created for each of the two SPLs. Additionally, we select (1) four prioritization techniques (Al-Hajjaji et al., 2017; Al-Hajjaji et al., 2014; Henard et al., 2014) that emphasize dissimilarity between products, such as in feature selection, to enhance coverage of elements or features, and (2) a testing order from previous work (Lity et al., 2017) that minimizes the overall differences in applied change operations captured in model regression deltas between successive variants. The chosen techniques are applicable because the necessary input artifacts, including delta sets and feature configurations, are available in this experiment. To achieve this, we employ the feature similarity (2014) and delta similarity (2017) techniques by Al-Hajjaji et al., the global maximum distance (GMD) and local maximum distance (LMD) methods from Henard et al. (2014), and the NEARIN algorithm from our earlier research (Lity et al., 2017).

text: We utilize quantitative data to validate our hypotheses, which are derived from the research questions. To determine if a hypothesis holds true, we employ the following data analysis procedures: RQ1 involves quantifying the unchanging, altered, and newly introduced variants identified by higher-order delta application reasoning during the transition to the subsequent SPL version under examination. RQ2 focuses on the number of retest goals produced by our change impact analysis (using incremental model slicing), where these goals signify that changes in the model affect previously tested behaviors across successive variants and their versions. RQ3 entails comparing the quantity of test cases selected and generated by our framework against those executed by the 'retest-all' method (Yoo and Harman, 2007) to ascertain any reduction in test cases. Furthermore, we evaluate the time expenditure for both types of change impact analyses to assess the efficiency of our selection approach, guided by the cost model by Leung and White (1991). RQ4 assesses our framework's fault detection rate relative to 'retest-all' (Yoo and Harman, 2007). As actual fault histories are unavailable for the two SPLs, we simulate faults by considering changes applied to a test model during transitions to subsequent variants or variant versions. Faults are generated by combining changes from model regression deltas (e.g., added transitions, source/target states of removed transitions) with randomly chosen transitions from the test model. These simulated faults represent incorrect artifact interactions caused by changes and their effect on shared behavior. For each variant and version, a corresponding set of simulated faults is created. Based on the fault set size, we generate various data sets, each involving a random selection of 10% of faults to create diverse random fault data sets. The test cases slated for retesting by our framework and those for 'retest-all' are then executed to determine the fault detection rate. RQ5, similar to RQ1, investigates the number of retest goals from our change impact analysis, which serve as an indicator of retesting potential. However, this RQ employs different testing orders. These orders are computed for initial SPL versions using established product prioritization techniques (e.g., Al-Hajjaji et al., 2017; Lity et al., 2017; Al-Hajjaji et al., 2014; Henard et al., 2014) and random generation. For random generation, 100 product orders are created for each SPL. Additionally, we choose (1) four prioritization techniques (Al-Hajjaji ets al., 2017, 2014; Henard et al., 2014) that prioritize product dissimilarity (e.g., in feature selection) to enhance coverage, and (2) a testing order from prior work (Lity et al., 2017) that minimizes overall differences in change operations between successive variants. These techniques are applicable due to the experiment's input requirements: delta sets and feature configurations. Specifically, we apply Al-Hajjaji et al.'s feature similarity (2014) and delta similarity (2017) techniques, Henard et al.'s (2014) global maximum distance (GMD) and local maximum distance (LMD) approaches, and the NEARIN algorithm from our previous work (Lity et al., 2017).

In order to create a feature selection optimization problem, values for the resource consumption and value of each feature must be generated. These values are created by generating pseudo-random numbers for the following problem parameters: (1) the resources consumed by each terminal feature r(tfi) = random(Rmax); (2) the resources consumed by each non-terminal feature r(nfi) = 0; (3) the value per unit resource that can be consumed by each terminal feature unitV = random(UnitVmax); (4) the value for each terminal feature v(tfi) = r(tfi) × unitV + random(Vmax); and (5) the value for each non-terminal feature v(nfi) = 0. Here, Rmax, UnitVmax, and Vmax are the upper bound on resource requirements, unit price of a resource, and the extra value of a feature after its consumed resource price. The value of each feature is not directly proportional to its resource consumption. The function random(i) returns an integer from 0 to (i − 1), following a uniform distribution. The total resources available for feature selections are then constrained to Rc = Rmax × nTF × 0.8 where nTF is the number of all terminal features in a feature model. ... For larger problems, we needed to generate problems for which we knew the optimal solution value. We used Akbar et al. (2001) test pattern generation technique to overcome this challenge. Akbar’s generation approach sets the problem parameters as follows: (1) a valid selection of terminal features is randomly chosen by the problem generator to serve as the optimal solution; (2) if S is the set of features randomly chosen to be in the optimal solution, then the generator sets R′(S) = R(S) = fi ∈ Sr(fi) so that the available resources exactly equal the resources needed for the optimal feature selection; and (3) the value associated with each of the randomly chosen optimal features is set to v′(fi) = r(fi) × unitV + Vmax. Thus V′(S) = fi ∈ Sv′(fi) = fi ∈ S(r(fi) × unitV + Vmax), which guarantees that there is no feature selection that fits within the resource constraints and has a higher value than the feature selection that the problem generator selected to serve as the optimal solution.

To construct a feature selection optimization problem, we generated values for each feature's resource consumption and overall value. These pseudo-random numbers were determined by: (1) r(tfi) = random(Rmax) for terminal feature resource consumption; (2) r(nfi) = 0 for non-terminal feature resource consumption; (3) unitV = random(UnitVmax) for terminal feature value per unit resource; (4) v(tfi) = r(tfi) × unitV + random(Vmax) for terminal feature value; and (5) v(nfi) = 0 for non-terminal feature value. Rmax, UnitVmax, and Vmax represent the upper limits for resource requirements, the unit cost of a resource, and the additional value of a feature beyond its consumed resource price, respectively. It's noteworthy that feature value is not directly proportional to resource consumption. The random(i) function produces an integer uniformly from 0 to (i − 1). The total resources available for feature selections were limited to Rc = Rmax × nTF × 0.8, where nTF is the number of all terminal features in the model. ... For larger problems, it was necessary to generate instances where the optimal solution value was already known. To overcome this, we utilized the test pattern generation technique developed by Akbar et al. (2001). Akbar's generation method sets problem parameters as follows: (1) the problem generator randomly selects a valid set of terminal features to serve as the optimal solution; (2) if S is the optimal set, the generator sets R′(S) = R(S) = fi ∈ Sr(fi) to ensure available resources exactly match those needed for the optimal feature selection; and (3) the value associated with each randomly chosen optimal feature is set to v′(fi) = r(fi) × unitV + Vmax. This results in V′(S) = fi ∈ Sv′(fi) = fi ∈ S(r(fi) × unitV + Vmax), guaranteeing that no other feature selection meeting resource constraints can achieve a higher value than the one chosen by the problem generator as optimal.

text: The optimality and the time consumption of a solution are measured as dependent variables. ... Optimality is defined as (Approximation Answer/Optimal Answer) to measure how close an algorithm can get to the optimal answer. Here, the Approximation Answer represents the total value of a solution produced by an approximation algorithm such as GAFES or FCF + M-HEU. Since BBLP is an exact technique, we use the total value of a solution produced by FCF + BBLP as the Optimal Answer. For example, for the same optimization problem (the same feature model, the same resource constraints, and the same optimization target), if GAFES obtains an approximate solution with the total value of 90 and FCF + BBLP obtains an optimal solution with the total value of 100, then the optimality of the GAFES solution is 90%. But finding exact solutions is NP-hard, which means that it is not feasible to apply FCF+BBLP to large feature models (e.g., number of features ≥ 500). Therefore, for large feature models (number of features ≥ 500), we used the test pattern generation technique devised by Akbar et al. (2001) to generate random optimization problem instances that we knew the optimal answer to (Section 7.1.2). The time consumption of a solution is measured by purely computing the running time of each algorithm (FCF + BBLP, FCF + M-HEU, and GAFES) to generate the solution. The startup time of the JVM and the time to generate the input feature model and the optimization problem instance are not considered. For example, the time consumption of a GAFES solution only comprises the running time of all steps described in Algorithm 1, i.e., the running time of population initialization and genetic iterations. Each genetic iteration is composed of chromosome selection, crossover, mutation, replacement, fitness evaluation, and our repair operator called FesTransform. To guarantee precision, we used Java’s System.nanoTime() to capture the start and stop time of GAFES and the other algorithms. The scalability of each algorithm (FCF + BBLP, FCF + M-HEU, and GAFES) was evaluated by measuring how the time consumption of each algorithm increased as the feature models increased in size. Based on a statistical analysis of the time consumption of each algorithm to solve for feature selections on different size feature models, we evaluated and compared the scalability of the three algorithms. An algorithm was considered more scalable if the rate of increase in solving time as it was fed larger and larger feature models was lower than another algorithm.

text: We have used three performance metrics to analyze the results of the evaluation. Hyper volume (HV) [55] is a very popular metric due to its good theoretical and practical properties, such as being compliant with Pareto dominance – if one population Pareto dominates another then it has a higher HV – and not requiring the problem’s Pareto front to be known. HV calculates the volume of the objective space between the obtained solution set and a reference point. A large value is preferable and reflects good performance of the solution set in terms of convergence, extensity and uniformity. We have also used the suitability of the final product as a metric. As aforementioned, this value is obtained through the analysis of several aspects of a product, including the opinion of the customers and the cost of the feature as per developers’ opinion. This is an innovation of this proposal and a metric to be compared among the several algorithms that may be inserted in the optimization phase of the approach. Finally, we have used the time spent to find the suggested products as metric too.

[30], we use three metrics to evaluate the quality of the configurations of the Pareto front: Hypervolume, Epsilon and Inverted Generational Distance. a) Hypervolume (HV): This metric represents the volume of the objective space that is dominated by the Pareto front A. b) Epsilon (E ): This metric measures the shortest distance that is required to transform every solution in a Pareto front A to dominate the reference front [30]. c) Inverted Generational Distance (IGD): This metric is the average distance from the solutions belonging to the reference front to the closest solution in a Pareto front A [34]. 2) Diversity Metrics: These metrics ensure that the decision maker has a variety of solutions to choose. We use two diversity metrics: the Pareto front size and the Spread of the solutions in the explored space. a) Pareto Front Size (PFS): This metric is the number of solutions in a Pareto front A. It is calculated as the cardinality of the Pareto front set, i.e., PFS(A) = jAj. A higher Pareto front size is preferred since more options are given to the user. However, this is only important when high quality is preserved. b) Spread (S): The spread measure defines the extent of spread in the solutions of the Pareto front A. In this study, we are measuring the following 5 objectives:1) Correctness. We seek to minimize the constraints of the FM that are violated by a configuration. 2) Richness of features. text: We evaluated the performance of the studied algorithms in terms of three aspects: (1) the quality of the approximate Pareto front produced, (2) the convergence to the exact Pareto front, and (3) the diversity of the solutions produced. As suggested by Zitzler et al. [60], we measured the quality of an approximate (Pareto) front using the following three metrics: – Hypervolume (HV) [6]. This metric calculates the volume of the subspace covered by an approximate front A. It evaluates how well the approximate front A fulfills the optimization objectives. A higher HV indicates a better Pareto front. – Epsilon (ε) [60]. This metric calculates the shortest dis- tance that is required to transform every solution in an approximate front A to dominate the reference front R. It evaluates how close an approximate front A is to the reference front R. A lower ε indicates a better Pareto front. – Inverted Generational Distance (IGD) [29]. This metric calculates theaveragedistancefromthesolutions belong- ing to the reference front R to the closest solution in an approximate front A. It complements the ε metric to eval- uate how close an approximate front A is to the reference front R. A lower IGD indicates a better Pareto front. We measured the convergence to the exact Pareto front using the following metric: – Error Ratio (ER) [32]. This metric calculates the percent- age of solutions in an approximate front A that are not solutions in the reference front R. It evaluates the pro- portion of non-true solution in an approximate front A. A lower ER indicates a better Pareto front. We measured the diversity using the following metric: – Generalized Spread (GS) [12]. This metric calculates the extent of spread in the solutions of an approximate front A. It evaluates the distribution of all solutions among all the optimization objectives. A higher GS indicates a better Pareto front.

text: Exp 1: To evaluate our research hypotheses, we used a between-subjects design, which means we split our sample in two groups and compared the performance between both groups, the ifdef group (21 subjects) and the color group (22 subjects). The ifdef group worked with the ifdef version, the color group worked with the color version of the source code. The method group (MG) used the integrated ARE instructions according to the template described in [2]. In contrast, the control group (CG) used traditional ARE instructions according to a VM-based ARE approach combined with a TORE [13] guideline. The SPL specification in which the main SPL features and the SPL architecture were described was given to all participants. Thus, the control group was equipped with state of the art material, while the method group was equipped with our novel approach. During the experiment, both groups performed fictitious but controlled elicitation interviews in order to gather requirements. The participants’ performance was measured using the aforementioned variables in order to enable statistical comparison. Each participant was randomly assigned to exactly one group. However, in order to assure equal distribution of REexperienced and less experienced participants in both groups, their RE background was taken into consideration. A statistical test showed that a significant difference regarding RE experience between the two groups could not be confirmed. text: Before the first trial, the researchers carried out a comparative analysis of the four models to establish the complexity of each feature model applying the following criteria: number of features, the maximum depth of features, and the amount of variability. Based on these three criteria, we categorize the feature models in two different complexity levels: normal complexity and more complex models. Thus, two domains were considered with normal complexity level (mobile devices and library, S01 and S02, respectively) and the other two models considered more complex (context-aware mobile applications and hospitality, C01 and C02, respectively) [de Mello et al., 2014]. Then, researchers evenly distributed all four domains to be inspected in both trials by each subject [de Mello et al., 2014]. However, after analyzing the results from the first trial, we observed that the complexity of the domains did not influence the performance of effectiveness/ efficiency in both trials. On the other hand, we noted that only the inspections performed over complex domains had their effectiveness significantly benefited through using FMCheck. Thus, in this trial, we arbitrary set C01 and C02 to be inspected only in the first trial (ad-hoc), while S01 and S02 were configured to be inspected only in the second trial (FMCheck).

text: We designed one external configuration for a Dr.Chat Mobile application shown in Fig. 14. We also built a scenario suite with a set of expected quality scenarios for a product under construction. The experiment is based on two transactions to be performed with a Dr.Chat Mobile application. The transactions represent a user’s stimulus from an application functional perspective (e.g. execute a consultation transaction). The first transaction (TR1) requires the application user to create and submit a medical consultation. The following steps comprise the transaction. Once the user is logged into the system, the application must locate the user (using either the device’s sensors or manual selection from the index-based lists). The user must then describe his medical condition using text and attachments, including voice or video recording and pictures. Finally, the application sends the consultation to the medical server. The second transaction (TR2) requires the application user to retrieve a previously submitted medical consultation and check its attachments. In this transaction, the user first selects a medical consultation from the medical record stored in cellphone’s memory, then retrieves from the server its attachments including voice or video recordings and pictures. Our experimental design contains two main parts. The first part (XP1) focuses on testing the human analyst’s behavior, while the second (XP2) tests SPAF assistance capabilities. In the first part (XP1), the human analyst must manually select a set of concrete components from the components in the core assets base to instantiate product architecture. Given a scenario suite, the analyst must then find possible sets of components that can fulfil the responses according to the stimulus in the quality scenarios in the context of (TR1) and (TR2). To test the selected components, the human analyst produce a product production plan for each set of components, and use the SPL to derive the product. For each product the suite tests are executed and using the monitoring tools she collects the top-rated ones according to its functional and quality characteristics. In the second part (XP2), the human analyst must model the Dr.Chat Mobile SPL software architecture, variability, component catalog, and scenario suite using the proposed languages for each domain provided by SPAF. The tester must also model one sensitivity point for each scenario in the provided suite case. The human analyst must then run the SPAF tool and collect the top-rated components according to its functional and quality characteristics. The analyst uses the components proposed by SPAF to define the product production plan and then use the SPL to derive the products. A detailed description of the test procedure, subjects, objects, and recording mechanisms is presented below.

text: To compare the performance of the three type-checking strategies, we applied each strategy to each subject system, and we measured the time required by every step of the type-checking procedure (i.e., tsetup and tchecking). We repeated each measurement 10 times and took the average value to reduce measurement bias. The maximum relative standard error was 3.1 %, which we observed for family- based type checking of ZIPME. For the product-based strategy, we did not include the time needed to generate the configuration of each product, because this time was negligible compared to the time required for type checking. Likewise, for the feature-based strategy, we did not include the time used to generate stubs (Sec- tion 2.4), because stubs represent required interfaces and are part of the corresponding feature modules. We measured the performance of the family-based type checker twice, with and without caching, to investigate the influence of the caching (Section 3.2) on the over- all performance. We instrumented the code of the FUJI compiler with calls to the timer of ThreadMXBean,4 such that we measure only the CPU time consumed by the type-checker thread. This approach eliminates the influence of other concurrent tasks (e.g., garbage collection) on the measurement results. Furthermore, we did not measure the JVM startup time for each type-checking run, because the overhead can be avoided using special tools.

text: D1: Neutral mentors. In order to perform the study, four neutral mentors were selected by the faculty teaching the course. The mentors had one-year teaching experience in software engineering. These mentors were trained in IVM by two colleagues of the author. The rationale behind the usage of mentors is to avoid interaction of the authors with the participants of the study (this prevented the authors to manipulate the participants of the study). Yin (2003) and Lee (1989) also emphasize the use of neutral mentors. D2: Assignment of participants to mentors. The 258 participants were divided randomly into four training groups consisting of about 60–70 participants. This was our high-level team creation. A trainer was assigned to each of the training groups, thus creating a one-to-one mapping between trainer and training group. The use of random sampling ensured a heterogeneous distribution of participants in each of the training groups (see SQ2). Each of the training group was decomposed into smaller groups to obtain fine granular teams (see D5). Issue-based variability management was taught to participants by the individual trainers. Overall, nineteen sessions were conducted to teach the rationale modeling approach to the participants. D3: Setting and unit of analysis with embedded design. Fig. 5 shows the organizational setup used for the quasi-experiment. To study the interaction of participants with IVM we considered a team of participants performing issue-based variability management as a unit of analysis. As the study included several instances of unit of analysis, our setting has an embedded design. The sample performing variability management in the project is the Setting. The setting consists of several objects of Unit of Analysis (which is a team performing issue-based variability management). These Units are observed by the Mentors. The participants are Actors (between 2 and 22) that perform issue-based variability management which is the unit of analysis of the experiment (see Fig. 6). The top-level Issue-based variability management is decomposed into three sub use cases Variability identification, Variability instantiation and Variability evolution. The first two optional sub use cases were included in Phase 1 and third optional sub use case was included in Phase 2. Both unit of analysis and embedded design are often used in case studies. Embedding a unit of analysis in the quasi-experimental setting: (i) enabled us to focus on the individual points of interests and (ii) additionally helped us to perform observations for collecting qualitative evidence. D4: The two phase approach. As instantiation and evolution of variability models are two different activities, we planned to analyze these activities separately in two phases (Phase 1 and Phase 2), which were performed chronologically one after the other. The two phase separation also helps us to study the reuse of rationale during the evaluation of ERP, that is, rationale captured during variability identification within a team in Phase 1 was used by a different team in Phase 2. The tasks for the two phases were already specified in Section 4.2. The students worked within the TU Munich campus. The participants worked on dedicated workstations throughout the project. This allows the mentors to observe the teams personally. In Phase 2, the participants did not have dedicated workstations; in fact, they worked at various distributed locations throughout campus. As a result, the mentors were not able to observe the students personally. D5: Creating teams. We replicated the unit of analysis several times with different team sizes and participants. Replications are considered to be critical for obtaining strong empirical evidence (Amir and Sharon, 1990). To realize a unit of analysis in Phase 1, we spitted the four high-level groups into low-level teams using convenience sampling. We provided nineteen time slots, with a mentor assigned to each slot. Each participant was asked to register for a slot that corresponds to their mentor from the training session. The number of participants in a slot was fixed (15–22 participants). In some slots, mentors further divided the participants randomly into smaller teams (team size < 6). In some other slots, mentors sampled large teams (8 ≤ team size ≤ 13). Due to problems with room availability, in some situations all students registered for a slot were used as a team (team size ≥ 15). Here, team size was very large. To ensure the heterogeneity of the participants in the various teams we used so called exercise teams in Phase 2. An exercise team was randomly created at the beginning of the software engineering course for performing the assignments of the software engineering lecture. In the following, we summarize teams that were created in the two phases (see Table 4): • In Phase 1, 42 teams were created with a team size between 2 and 22. The reason for the large number of teams was to study the impact of team size on the quality of instantiation. • In Phase 2, we defined 50 teams consisting of 2–6 students. Having smaller team sizes compared with Phase 1 enabled us to study the reuse of rationale closely. Domain and application engineering were separated in each of the team. All decisions were made using the issue-based communication. D6: Variables measured. The independent and dependent variables, the corresponding study question and the variability management activity are summarized in Table 5. No variables were defined for measuring SQ2, because it was evaluated based on qualitative data. We validated how the rationale captured by a team in Phase 1 is reused (ERP) in a different team of Phase 2. Therefore, Quality of rationale is measured during variability identification and Reuse of rationale is measured during variability evolution. Other variables such as Motivation of participants, Team size and Quality of instantiation were measured Phase 1.

text: As presented in [20,27], due to the complexity of large feature models resulting in configurations of thousands of features, it is very important to measure the response time and the scalability of feature models algorithms. Furthermore, in our case as we deal with cardinality-based feature models, where small feature models can produce really large and complex configurations, the scalabil- ity issue is even more important. Operators defined over feature models have to demonstrate their scalability in terms of the num- ber of features [20,27], normally using randomly generated feature models. In our case, we refer to configurations with cloned fea- tures, so we have to prove the scalability of the proposed algo- rithms in terms of the number of clones of the configurations. In order to demonstrate this, we could use a unique feature model (i.e. the feature model of FamiWare middleware), and simply vary the size of the generated configurations. Instead of generating ran- dom configurations we consider it more useful to experiment with the configurations generated from real case studies (e.g. a smart home) as we will show later. So, we will show that Hydra with its evolution operators works well with concrete case studies con- sidering a large number of cloned features, representing the num- ber of devices that can be interconnected in typical AmI systems. The time needed to create a configuration depends on the num- ber of clonable features selected for the configurations. Since in FamiWare, the clonable feature is the Device, the time needed to create a configuration depends very much on the number of de- vices connected in the same AmI system. Although the evolution process presented here can be applied to any SPL, in the scope of this paper, we did our experiments with several instantiations of FamiWare for different case studies. Spe- cifically, we have implemented several versions of smart homes, AAL homes and ITSs, which were evolved using our evolution pro- cess with expected results as Table 1 shows. ... Our algorithms are not so complex, but it is better to verify their correctness in order to ensure that the evolution process does not introduce any errors. It is possible to prove the correctness of our algorithms either (i) via their execution with different case studies or (ii) via some kind of formal reasoning. We have performed both kinds of correctness verifications. Firstly, we used both operators of Hydra to evolve the four case studies in Table 1, but taking into account only a few features were added and removed. We repeated the same experiments, but we evolved the configurations manually. On the other hand, we have applied the differences and cre- ate_configuration algorithms separately to the case studies in Table 1, obtaining consistent results. Following the semantic definition of the create_configuration operator, the new configuration is the pre- vious configuration where the features of the UNS set are removed and the features of the SEL set are added ðNC 1⁄4 ðPC n UNSÞ [ SELÞ. Then, for every case study in Table 1, we have used the create_con- figuration facility of Hydra for evolving the previous configurations and creating new ones giving the UNSi and SELi sets as inputs. After this step, we have a new configuration (NC) for each previous con- figuration (PC). Then, taking advantage of the fact that both algo- rithms are complementary (i.e. the differences algorithm return the UNS and SEL sets between PC and NC; SEL 1⁄4 NC n PC and UNS 1⁄4 PC n NC), we execute the differences algorithm for every cou- ple of PC and NC getting as outputs the UNSj and SELj sets. Then we check that UNSi is equal UNSj and that SELi is equal SELj, which means that at least both algorithms give consistent results. Furthermore, in order to demonstrate the correctness of the cre- ate_configuration algorithm we have modelled this problem with a CSP taking advantage of the Choco Library used by Hydra. What we need to prove is that the semantic definition of the create_configu- ration operator, which is: NC 1⁄4 ðPC n UNSÞ [ SEL, specified in CSP gives the same results as our algorithm. A CSP is defined by a trip- let (X, D, C), where X is the set of variables of the problem, D is a function that associates the domain to each variable, and C is a set of constraints. In our case, the variables are the names of the features, the domain is 0 for the non-selected features and 1 for the selected features of a configuration and the constraints are the semantic definition of the create_configuration operator: ðPC n UNSÞ [ SEL. ... Here we have applied the results of the operators to evolve our middleware, but it can be used to evolve other kinds of systems de- fined using feature models and specifically cardinality-based fea- ture models. The evolution process presented here is able to manage changes produced in configurations with clones, at design time. But, in general, SPL engineering processes can also be applied at runtime, as proposed in the Dynamic Software Product Lines [28] (DSPL) approach. Following a DSPL approach, we extended the FamiWare middleware to support dynamic reconfiguration using the operators presented here. The details of how the recon- figuration is defined in FamiWare using these operators can be found in [29,30]. We use the create_configuration operator to obtain the next configuration at runtime, after a new context situation re- quires the evolution of the running system. Also, we use the differ- ence operator to generate implementation level plans that must be executed at runtime to make the system evolve to a next configu- ration from a previous one.

text: This experiment was performed through a number of iterative steps. In each step, we randomly generated 5000 feature models and checked their consistency, saving the maximum fitness ob- tained. Then, we executed ETHOM and allowed it to run for the same number of executions of the fitness function (5000) and com- pared the results. Recall that the size of the population in our algo- rithm was set to 200 individuals which meant that the maximum number of generations was 25, i.e., 5000/200. This process was re- peated with different model sizes to evaluate the scalability of our algorithm. In particular, we generated models with different com- binations of features, {200, 400, 600, 800, 1000} and percentage of constraints (with respect to the number of features), {10%, 20%, 30%, 40%}. The maximum branching factor was set to 10 in all the experiments. For each model size, we repeated the process 25 times to get averages and performed statistical analysis on the data. In total, we performed about 5 million executions3 of the fitness function for this experiment. The fitness was set to be the number of backtracks used by the analysis tool when checking the model consistency. For the analysis, we used the solver JaCoP integrated into FaMa v1.0 with the default heuristics MostCon- strainedDynamic for the selection of variables and IndomainMin for the selection of values from the domains. To prevent the experiment from getting stuck, a maximum timeout of 30 min was used for the execution of the fitness function in both the random and evolution- ary search. If this timeout was exceeded during random generation, the execution was cancelled and a new iteration was started. If the timeout was exceeded during evolutionary search, the best solution found until that moment was returned, i.e., the instance exceeding the timeout was discarded. After all the executions, we measured the execution time of the hardest feature models found for a full comparison, i.e., those producing a larger number of backtracks. More specifically, we executed each returned solution 10 times to get average execution times. ... The experiment consisted of a number of iterative steps. At each step, we randomly generated 5000 models and compiled each of them into a BDD for use in counting the number of solutions of the input feature model. We then executed ETHOM and allowed it to run for 5000 executions of the fitness function (i.e., 25 gener- ations) searching for feature models maximising the size of the BDD. Again, this process was repeated with different combinations of features, {50, 100, 150, 200, 250} and percentages of constraints, {10%, 20%, 30%} to evaluate the scalability of our approach. For each model size, we repeated the process 25 times to get statistics from the data. In total, we performed about 3.5 million executions of the fitness function for this experiment. We may remark that we generated smaller feature models than those presented in the pre- vious experiment in order to reduce BDD building time and make the experiment affordable. Measuring memory usage in Java is dif- ficult and computationally expensive since memory profilers usu- ally add a significant overload to the system. To simplify the fitness function, we decided to measure the fitness of a model as the num- ber of nodes of the BDD representing it. This is a natural option used in the research community to compare the space complexity of BDD tools and heuristics (Mendonca et al., 2008). For the analy- sis, we used the solver JavaBDD (2013) integrated into the feature model analysis tool SPLOT (Mendonca et al., 2009). We chose SPLOT for this experiment because it integrates highly efficient ordering heuristics specifically designed for the analysis of feature models using BDDs. In particular, we used the heuristic ‘Pre-CL- MinSpan’ presented by Mendonca et al. in Mendonca et al. (2008). For a detailed description of the configuration of the solver we refer the reader to Segura et al. (2013). As in our previous experiment, we set a maximum timeout of 30 min for the fitness function to prevent the experiment from getting stuck. We mea- sured the compilation and execution time of the hardest feature models found to allow a more detailed comparison. Each optimal solution was compiled and executed 10 times to get average times.

text: We set the characteristics of generated feature models as: 50%, 25%, and 25% for probability of being features in AND, OR, and XOR groups, respectively. Moreover, 50% of features in AND groups are optional features. The branching factor is also set to 10. These characteristics are backed up by most of surveyed feature models [32] [33] to reflect the characteristics of real feature models. Generating optimal configurations based on the stakeholders’ preferences and constraints is NP-hard. Hence, HTN planners similar to CSP solvers have problems in finding optimal solution for large-scale problems. Although the SHOP2 planner applies some heuristics for improving search time for finding an optimal plan (See ref. [5]), due to explicit representations of states in the memory, SHOP2 runs into memory problems for large domains. However, our experiments showed for feature models with size of 200, SHOP2 returns an optimal plan in feasible time. According to the results of investigation on non-functional properties done by [12], the number of relevant non-functional properties for different application domains is at most 11. Moreover, Sommerville and Sawyer [13] highlighted that the effective number of non-functional properties is around six. Considering these two studies, we defined 10 non-functional properties; six quantitative; and four qualitative non-functional properties. Five qualifier tags were defined for each non-functional property. For each feature model, we applied our tool to configure the feature model based on preferences and constraints. To configure the feature models, we considered three independent variables including number of features, number of constraints, and integrity constraints; and time as a dependent variable. For each feature model in the study, features were annotated with quantitative non-functional properties and their values were produced by a random function with normal distribution. From a practical point of view, only some of features (not all) may have impact on a qualitative NFP like security. Hence, to reflect this point, features were randomly annotated with 0 to 4 qualitative non-functional properties with normal distribution, that is, most of the features had one or two non-functional properties. Based on our analysis on SPLOT repository [7], which shows average of 18% of integrity constraints for the real feature models [31], we considered two distributions of integrity constraints: 10% and 20%. Finally, for the constraints over NFPs, four cases were considered: no constraint and constraints over 2,4, and 6 NFPs to reflect the effect of various constraints over NFPs at run time.

text: For the needs of the experiment, the t-sets of the FMs for t 3 are computed using the following procedure. First, a list of all the features of the FM is recovered. Then, all the possible t-sets are enumerated and provided to the solver to determine whether they are valid or not. For the large FMs, computing the exact number of valid t-sets is a non-trivial and time consuming task. For instance, it took around three days to a 10-threaded program running on our system to compute the 92,540,449 valid 2-sets of the Linux FM. As t increases, the number of valid t-sets explodes. As a result, we estimate the number of t-sets. To this end, 1,000 t-wise sets are randomly sampled and checked. Since the total number of possible t-sets of an FM is known and equal to 2n t for n features (2n because each feature is either selected or unselected), the valid t-sets can be directly estimated (law of large numbers). _RQ1: We compare our generation approach with the three tools. We also consider CASA where the desired number of configurations can be specified. This approach is denoted as CASA-n. We employ the 10 real FMs of moderate size. For each FM and for t ¼ 2; . . . ; 6, the three approaches are executed. Then, if the result is available, our approach and CASA-n are performed with the parameters corresponding to the minimum number of configurations provided by the other tehcniques. Similarly, the running time of our approach was set to the minimum one. CASA, CASA-n and our search-based approach are performed 10 times independently as they are heuristic techniques providing different solutions at each execution. _RQ2: To enable a fair comparison, the searchbased and unpredictable approaches generate sets of configurations of the same size as those provided by SPLCAT. The search-based approach is allowed to run for one minute and is performed 10 times per FM. For the 100 generated FMs, the results presented are averaged on all the FM. To estimate the t-wise coverage of the product configurations, we use a process similar as the one used to calculate the t-sets of an FM and described in the beginning of Section 7. The sampling process is repeated 10 times per each examined t value (t ¼ 2 to t ¼ 6) with samples of size 100,000. The search-based and unpredictable approaches are executed on all the large FMs to produce five times 50 and 100 configurations, with the time restriction of 30 minutes. Another experiment involves the generation of 1,000 configurations and the recording of the coverage over the runs of the search-based approach. _RQ3 e RQ4: For each moderate FMs, three different sets of configurations are used to apply the prioritization techniques. The first set is the set of configurations produced by SPLCAT (Case I). The second one is a set of n configurations, where n ¼ #features 2 , selected with the unpredictable method (Case II). Finally, the last set is composed of the configurations generated by SPLCAT plus the same amount of configurations selected by the unpredictable method (Case III). Using these different sets allows ensuring that the prioritization approaches are relevant whatever the nature of the configurations. All these sets of configurations are randomized before executing the prioritization techniques. This practice ensures that our approaches are independent of the original order. On each of the three cases and for each FM, a random prioritization is averaged 10 times. Cases II and III are independently repeated 10 times to avoid any bias from the initial set of configurations. For each approach and each independent repetition, the execution time is recorded. We generate two sets of 100 and 500 configurations containing dissimilar configurations (Case IV) and two sets of the same sizes containing half similar and dissimilar configurations (Case V). We choose these two kinds of sets of configurations since the prioritization approaches are similarity-driven and can thus be influenced by the nature of the used sets. Indeed, applying these approaches on sets containing dissimilar configurations can be less effective than applying them on sets containing similar configurations. We randomize each set of configurations and execute the Local MaximumDistance and Global Maximum Distance prioritizations on each of them. We also produce 10 random orderings to compare with our approaches. This practice shows that the prioritization techniques are not affected by random orders.

text: l) Creating the MPFM: We analyzed 6 different portals of site X and made a list of their features. We also chose another internationalized website Y, similar to site X, for our analysis. The purpose of choosing one more site was to ensure that the resulting model is a representation of the domain rather than a single product. A feature list for this site also was made. An analysis of these feature lists revealed that there were many features in common while some of them varied across different instances. We used this information to build the domain feature model. Each portal of site X would be a product configuration, however we do not create the configurations yet, because the perspectives are still to be created. Next we identified the perspectives. This was done by identifying common causes of variation. Since each portal is country specific, many features vary by country. Here are some examples: the feature “top news of the hour” is seen English on the UK site and in Arabic in the UAE site, the weather update is shown in Celsius in the UK site and in Fahrenheit in the USA site, stock updates are shown in US Dollar on the USA site and in Indian Rupee on the India site. All these examples are of different variations due to the same cause i.e. Country. Hence this is a candidate for making a perspective. We created this separate feature tree and named it as the internationalization perspective. Next we create the association named “Source of Variation” to link the domain feature to the variation. In our examples above “Top news in the hour” from the domain perspective is linked to “Language” in the internationalization perspective similarly “Stock update” from the domain perspective is linked to “Currency” from the internationalization perspective. Another example of a perspective we could identify was that of Architecture. We observed that the same domain feature could be configured on different kinds of architectural components. For example, the advertising module could be shown in the second column of a 2 page layout or on the third column of a 3 page layout. The advertising feature varies here by the page layout used. Similarly we observed variations in page themes, page types (like blog type, news article type) etc. All of these are architectural components, hence we clubbed them under the Architectural perspective. In this process we realized that some kinds of variation like language and browser apply to all features. It is inefficient to create associations from all domain features to these. These had to be handled differently during generation. This has been explained in next subsection. In all we could identify 4 perspectives viz. Architecture, internationalization, accessibility, operating environment in addition to the domain perspective which contains the basic functionality features. A total of 150 features were created across all perspectives. The MPFM is now ready to be used for configuring the products. For our case we have chosen to consider each portal as a separate product. Product configurations are created by selecting features from the domain model. The tool ensures that constraints from the model are adhered when selection is done. For example, if a feature is associated with XOR operator then only one of its child features may be selected, if a parent feature is selected then all its mandatory child features are automatically selected etc. We created configurations for 4 countries for our evaluation. _2) Generating feature interactions: The MPFM is used as the input model for combinatorial test generation. Each perspective viz. domain, architecture, internationalization, accessibility, operating environment is a parameter to ACTS. Further we had found some features like browser, language, operating system which are sources of variation for all the domain features. We selected these also as parameters. The leaf nodes of each of these feature trees were used as the values for the respective parameters. We treat the domain feature as the one being tested and features from all other perspectives as the context in which it is being tested. The tool will ensure that a feature combination is valid by finding the product configuration which has all the features in the combination generated. There are cases where multiple configurations have the same combination. Hence product configuration i.e. portal was also one of the parameters to ACTS. Feature combinations that do not exist in any product are not generated at all. This is done by generating the relevant constraints and passing them to ACTS during test generation. Table II shows the parameters and values that were identified when a feature “Social Site integration” was being tested.

text: Both IBEA and GIA have some element of randomness in them, and so multiple runs must be used to get good measurements. For IBEA, we generated 1000 di↵erent parameters set- tings using Sobol sampling of four parameters: crossover rate from 0 to 1, mutation rate from 0 to 1, maximum num- ber of evaluations considered from 10,000 to 250,000, and population size from 10 to 1000. For each parameter setting, we ran IBEA 25 times with di↵erent random seeds on each run. text: To reduce the fluctuations in the dependent variable caused by the random generation, we performed 200 repetitions for each configuration of independent parameters, i.e., we generated 200 random FMs with the same parameters and each performed the same number of random operations of the same kind. ... The algorithm to randomly generate FMs of size n is as follows (Thum et al., 2009): starting with a single root node, it runs several iterations. In each iteration, an existing node without children is randomly selected, and one to ten (random amount) of child nodes are added. Those child nodes are connected either by And- (50% probability), Or- (25% probability) or Alternative-group (25% prob- ability). Children in an And-group are optional by a 50% probabil- ity. This iteration is continued until the FM has n features. All features with children are considered non-terminal. Moreover, we also generate cross-tree constraints (requires and excludes). For every 10 features, one constraint is generated by the following algorithm: two different features are randomly selected, and then are connected randomly by requires (50% probability) or excludes (50% probability) link. ... We fixed the following parameters: maximum number of chil- dren = 10; type of child group = (50%,25%,25%); optional child = 50%; number of cross-tree constraints = 0.1 ⁄ n; variables in cross-tree constrains = 2. According to Thum’s survey (Thum et al., 2009), these parameters are backed up by most of the sur- veyed FMs and represent a rough average. Thus, these generated FMs basically reflect the characteristics of realistic FMs. ... We randomly generated operations on an FM as well. Our generator takes an FM and the number of operations as input. The 20 primitive operations defined in Table 2 are implemented. They are classified as three main types: ‘add’, ‘remove’, and ‘set’. Our generator can limit the kind of input operations to ‘add’, ‘remove’, ‘set’, or ‘arbitrary’. For a fixed number of input operations, ‘arbitrary’ operations are composed of ‘add’ (33% probability), ‘remove’ (33% probability), and ‘set’ (33% probabil- ity) operations.

text: One of the important notes that need to be mentioned is that we use a ten-fold cross-validation approach [37], which is a method for estimating the performance of a predictive model, in order to evaluate the performance of our decision support platform. For this purpose, each of the domain documents are split into two segments with a size ratio of 9 to 1: the training segment (9/10) and a testing segment (1/10). The training segments of the documents are used in the NER learning stage, while the testing segments are used in our experiments with the domain experts. The reason for this is that if both the training and testing documents are equivalent, then the accuracy of the results is not reliable because it cannot be inferred whether the results of the experiments performed using our decision support platform is generalizable to unforseen documents or not. The cross-validation approach allows for such generalization. During the experiments, each participant was provided with two domain documents (The details of the two documents, D1 and D2, are shown in Table 4) from the test documents. The same two documents were provided to all of the participants. The task of the participants was to individually read the two documents, understand the content and then design a feature model based on the content of each document. So, the artifacts produced by each partici-pant after the end of the experiment were two feature models, one for each domain document. Now, in order to evaluate the impact of the decision support platform, each of the participants were asked to perform the process for one document using the decision support platform and the other one without the intervention of the decision support platform. In order to form a fair distribution, eight of the participants were asked to process D1 with the help of the decision support system and D2 without it, while the other seven participants were asked to perform otherwise. In addition, the first group of eight participants processed D1 first and then processed D2; therefore, they interacted with the decision support system in their first domain engineering experiment, whereas the second set of participants first performed the domain engineering process without the help of the decision support platform on D1 and were later able to use it while working on D2. This experiment setting was used in order to minimize the impact of the documents, their order, and the order of the use of the decision support platform on the performance of the participants and hence on the obtained observations.

text: In order to assure the success of the experiment, the entire design and setup material was carefully analyzed by both RE experts and empirical research experts prior to experiment execution. After incorporating the received feedback, a student assistant was coached with the list of prepared requirements and interruption questions, as she had to play the role of a (fictitious) stakeholder who provides its requirements during the experiment. In order to check whether the material was understandable for the participants (who should play the role of a requirements engineer) and the fictitious stakeholder, and whether the scheduled timeframe was sufficient, we then performed a pilot run with two bachelor students. Thus, a pretest with the method group’s material and one with the control group’s material was carried out. The observations during this pretest were used to finally improve the material. The experiment was split into 26 sessions of 90 minutes. The participants performed the experiment individually, as it was neither meaningful nor possible to let multiple participants perform elicitation interviews in parallel. In order to avoid the threat that one participant informs other participants about purpose, procedure, or material of the study, the participants had to sign a non-disclosure agreement that forbid them to disclose information until the end of the entire study. Further, before letting the participants perform the actual experiment, we used the pre-questionnaire for getting data about their experience, and for assigning them to a suitable group. After group assignment, the participants received a package with the experiment material. Each participant could then use the first 35 minutes to become familiar with the material, before the actual experiment took place. This time was experienced as being sufficient because the students in the pretests needed less than 25 minutes both. In this experiment, the participants were asked to perform an elicitation role-play (in English) in which the fictitious stakeholder had to be interviewed using the provided material. The participants were asked to follow the provided elicitation instructions and to consider the SPL specification, if required (see Figure 2). The fictitious stakeholder stated the corresponding requirements that had been prepared during study planning and that were aligned with an observer checklist. To minimize threats due to differences in her behavior, we assured that she was not informed about which group a participant was assigned to. The fictitious stakeholder also posed questions to the participants; for instance, about the feasibility and costs of certain requirements. This was done in order to increase the representativeness of the study for elicitation sessions in the real world, as an interview in practice is never just a pure one-way communication. The purpose of these interruptions was to check whether the participants were able to provide sufficient information in order to make the elicitation more realistic. An observer (played by the 1st author of this paper) tracked the interview questions asked by the participants, their reactions (i.e., acceptance or rejection) to the requirements of the fictitious stakeholder, as well as the answers to the fictitious stakeholder’s interrupting questions using the aligned observer checklist. Hence, for each prepared requirement and interrupting question, there was a check item on the list in order to track whether the participants asked for this requirement, respectively how they reacted on it. The reason for using observations and not any specified results was that requirements elicitation and no specification was subject of our investigation. In particular, the likely heterogeneity in the quality of the participants’ notes would probably have had a high impact on the evaluation so that no sound conclusion about elicitation performance could have been derived. By using the filled observer checklists, the aforementioned metrics could be clearly determined by comparing it with the sample solution. In this regard, the usage of prepared requirements and a corresponding observer checklist aimed at making the results comparable, which would otherwise have been a significant threat to validity. Further, in order to avoid missing observations, the entire elicitation role-play was recorded using a voice recorder. The complete role-play took about 30 minutes on average in both groups. In a last step, the participants were asked to fill out a post-questionnaire in which they were asked to assess the helpfulness of the material.
